focus: How should a board holding several diagrams be composed - titles, sections, legends, reading order and spacing between diagrams - so a reader meets it in the intended order?
answeredQuestions: How should a board holding several diagrams be composed — titles, sections, legends, reading order and spacing between diagrams — so a reader meets it in the intended order?

label: The packet states that a FigJam file has one page; Figma's documentation says FigJam files can contain multiple pages with no limit. The rule survives because no plugin write can add a page (createPage throws in FigJam), but the sentence should say that a tool cannot add a page while a person can, since that difference is what lets a multi-diagram board grow past one canvas.

A FigJam section can be created around objects that already exist (select, right-click, Create section), and sections exist to cluster objects without grouping them, so a generated diagram can be grouped with no node moving; the packet's prohibition on a section wrapping a generated node protects against appendChild, which is the wrong affordance for a diagram that already exists.

Sections bring four board-level capabilities the packet uses none of - contain as a movable unit, hide and reveal, deep link to a section, and set a section as the file thumbnail - and each maps to a quality the scorecard already scores: grouping, object integrity, appendix without competition, reply targeting, and the board's own first glance in the file browser.

Section titles are first-class (edit via toolbar or double-click, removable), and Figma's own board skill clears a section name when a title text exists inside it, so a board has exactly two title mechanisms and must pick one per region; the packet has neither, writing a floating charcoal text node only when an extension was requested.

Section locking (Lock all, or Lock background only keeping content editable) is the missing safety mechanism that would let a diagram be generated inside its own section without the appendChild move the packet fears; recorded as a route to verify rather than a fact, because no source states what the hosted generator does against a locked region.

Multi-diagram composition already has a published shape - one outer board section, one zone section per diagram, 92px between sibling sections in a row and 120px between rows, with 68/60/100/80 inner padding - which the packet can adopt directly; today it states no spacing figure at all between two diagrams.

Every source describes a reading order for a board and none describes a way to signal it: Figma fixes left-right/top-bottom with context, evidence, asks and appendix; the composition grammar fixes first, second and last glance; a published architecture-diagramming deck asks for a diagram understandable in seconds and standalone. A numbered section title is the cheapest available signal and costs nothing the packet forbids.

Mermaid layout hints mostly do nothing: none of them places a node, the & syntax does not group, extra dashes extend an edge but are not implemented in ELK, invisible links move nodes unpredictably, a subgraph constrains contents but adds a box, sibling subgraph declaration order renders reversed, and node declaration order is subordinate to the crossing-minimisation objective.

Because the FigJam generator is ELK-based, the extra-dash length hint is unavailable, leaving exactly three model-side levers: direction (already used), node declaration order (unused), and the edge set plus subgraph presence (used only for lanes). Reshape-the-model guidance should be rewritten as those three levers with their limits.

Sibling subgraphs render in reverse declaration order, so a process whose lanes are declared in working order can land with lanes reversed, and the packet's read-back counts lanes and checks containment but never lane order - a board can pass read-back while reading right-to-left through a process.

A published design source separates micro from macro whitespace - micro being the small space between shapes, lines, titles and icons - which names the two spacing systems a board needs at once: the 60-92/200-400/1000+ bands are macro whitespace, and the node gap the packet cannot measure is micro.

IBM's technical-diagram guidance pairs colour with labels or line styles for colour-blind readers, which the packet does only partly: it refuses to let colour carry meaning alone but encodes group membership with fill and stroke and gives no line-style channel, although the stroke dash vocabulary already exists in the comparator.

Crossings are a property of the graph, not only of the renderer - a published layout skill classifies nearly planar topology as a graph class before choosing a renderer - so the packet could flag must-cross edge pairs in its existing pre-write script and split or re-rank before the write instead of discovering crossings from a screenshot after it.

direction: Ask the generator to lay out a whole multi-diagram board in one call
reason: The tool draws one diagram per call and a plugin cannot create a FigJam page, so composition must happen in the section layer around the calls.

direction: Use & or invisible links as grouping syntax
reason: Mermaid documents that & does not group and invisible links are unpredictable; proposing them would violate the packet's never-invent rule.

direction: Treat the packet's one-page sentence as correct and build on it
reason: The rule stays but the reason is wrong; a later change must not repeat it.
